title: Incapacity — Organisational Process Flow
subtitle: Poor work performance · Ill health and injury · Incarceration · Incompatibility · Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 and the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294) · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an employer what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment a manager first sees that an employee may not be able to do the job until the matter closes and lessons feed back into policy. It covers the four forms of incapacity the Code now recognises, each with its own test, on one shared spine:

notes.text: Every case moves through the same phases: identification and classification; a type-specific investigation and support track; a structured search for alternatives short of dismissal; an incapacity enquiry only where dismissal remains possible; a reasoned outcome with referral rights; and governance. The flow assumes no collective agreement or bargaining council procedure applies, and must be adjusted where one does.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The fairness of a dismissal for incapacity is governed by the LRA (ss.185, 186(1), 187, 188 and 192). The employer must prove that the reason relates to the employee’s capacity and that a fair procedure was followed (s.188(1), s.192(2)). Action short of dismissal, such as a unilateral demotion or a dispute about training, is tested as an unfair labour practice under s.186(2)(a). The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (“the Code”), issued under s.203 and in effect from 4 September 2025, repealed the Schedule 8 Code of Good Practice: Dismissal. The Code is guidance, not statute, but anyone considering whether a dismissal was for a fair reason or in accordance with a fair procedure must take it into account (s.188(2), s.203(3)). Where the incapacity is a disability, the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 (EEA) applies alongside, and a dismissal on that ground without justification is automatically unfair (LRA s.187(1)(f)). Work-related injury and disease also engage COIDA and the Rehabilitation, Reintegration and Return-to-Work Regulations, 2026 (GN R.7205, GG 54273, 6 March 2026) (“RRR Regs”). A review on 15 October 2026 found no amendment to the Code since publication. The Labour Law Amendment Bill, 2025 (published for comment on 26 February 2026) would change this area if enacted, but it is a draft and not law (see 6.6). Status should be re-checked before this flow is adopted.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LRA = the Labour Relations Act and other statutes and regulations (BCEA, EEA, COIDA and RRR Regs, POPIA and its Health Information Regulations, 2026, OHS Act); binding now.
Code = the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (cited by item number); must be taken into account, and departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Incapacity is managed, not charged. The questions are always the same: what exactly can the employee not do; why; for how long; what would help; and what can the employer reasonably do short of dismissal. Dismissal is the last step of a documented search for alternatives, never the first response to a problem. The clock starts on the day any manager first sees the problem, because delay both prejudices the employee (who loses time to improve, recover or make arrangements) and weakens the employer’s case. Internal targets sit inside every statutory limit.

notes.heading: Eight interpretation points that shape the flow
points: The weight of the Code. The Code is intentionally general and departures “may be justified in proper circumstances” (item 2(1)); it does not alter rights under a collective agreement (item 2(3)); and it must not be read as requiring small businesses to do what is impractical (item 3). A recognition agreement or bargaining council procedure prevails over this flow. Record any justified departure at the time.

Can’t or won’t. Incapacity is an inability or unsuitability that is not a culpable breach of a rule; misconduct is a culpable breach (items 7 to 10). The same facts can point either way: poor output because the employee cannot do the work is incapacity; poor output because the employee will not do it is misconduct. Screen first (step 1.5) and choose one route; if facts emerge that change the picture, switch routes openly and restart the relevant protections. Where an employee with a known mental illness is alleged to have committed misconduct, investigate whether the illness affected their capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of the conduct or to act accordingly before deciding the route (BP). In law the employee bears the evidential burden on that point, and the illness may otherwise go to mitigation (CL: Legal Aid South Africa v Jansen [2020] ZALAC 37; New Way Motor & Diesel Engineering v Marsland, LAC 2009).

Four separate tests. Poor performance is tested against a known, reasonably achievable standard and a fair opportunity to meet it (items 19–20). Ill health is tested by the extent, duration and cause of the incapacity and the alternatives short of dismissal (item 21(1)–(5)). Incarceration is tested by the extent of the incapacity and the alternatives (item 21(6)). Incompatibility is tested by whether the employee cannot work in harmony with the business culture or colleagues, and whether that can be remedied (item 21(7)). Using the wrong test is the most common substantive error.

Temporary, permanent and “unreasonably long”. For ill health and incarceration, the first question is duration. A temporary incapacity calls for an investigation of its extent; if the employee is likely to be absent for a time that is unreasonably long in the circumstances, the Code provides that the employer should investigate all alternatives short of dismissal, weighing the nature of the job, the period of absence, the seriousness of the condition and the possibility of a temporary replacement (item 21(1)); a failure to do so will rarely be justified. A permanent incapacity calls for a search for alternative employment or adapted duties (item 21(2)). What is “unreasonably long” is fact-specific; this flow sets review points, not a fixed number of days.

Disability overlay. Many ill-health cases involve a disability. The employer must not unfairly discriminate on the ground of disability (EEA s.6(1)) and must reasonably accommodate a person with a disability unless that would impose unjustifiable hardship (EEA definition of “reasonable accommodation”; Code of Good Practice on the Employment of Persons with Disabilities, GN 1085, GG 39383, 9 November 2015). A dismissal is not automatically unfair if the reason is based on an inherent requirement of the job (LRA s.187(2)(a)). Medical testing is prohibited unless legislation permits or requires it or it is justifiable (EEA s.7, verify wording); HIV testing needs Labour Court authorisation (EEA s.7(2)). Health information is special personal information (POPIA s.26). An employer may process it for the reintegration of, or support for, workers in connection with sickness or work incapacity (s.32(1)(f)), but only through persons bound by a duty of confidentiality (s.32(2)), and subject to the Regulations relating to the Processing of Data Subjects’ Health Information by Certain Responsible Parties, 2026 (GN 7198, GG 54268, 6 March 2026), which set confidentiality, security-safeguard and secure-disposal requirements for health records.

Work-related incapacity. The duty to accommodate is more onerous for employees injured at work or incapacitated by a work-related illness (item 21(5)). Run the GBS COIDA flow in parallel; before dismissing or reducing the pay of an employee on a COIDA claim, the RRR Regs require: notice to the Compensation Fund or Licensee of an intention to dismiss or reduce pay (reg 10(1)(n)); a written report of any dismissal, with reasons, to the Chief Inspector and the Fund or Licensee (reg 10(1)(m)); written notice of resumption of duty or of inability to retain the employee (reg 10(1)(o)); and retention of RRR reports for at least 30 years (reg 10(1)(d)).

Counting time and pay. Sick leave is a statutory entitlement over a 36-month cycle (BCEA s.22): the days the employee would normally work in 6 weeks per cycle or, in the first 6 months, 1 day for every 26 days worked (s.22(2)–(3)) and the employer may require a medical certificate for absence of more than two consecutive days or on more than two occasions in eight weeks (BCEA s.23(1)); a valid certificate must be issued and signed by a medical practitioner or another person certified to diagnose and treat patients and registered with a professional council established by an Act of Parliament (s.23(2)). Once paid sick leave is exhausted, the employee is on unpaid sick leave, not absent without leave; UIF illness benefits (UIA s.20) may be claimed for illness of 7 days or more once paid sick leave is exhausted. An incarcerated employee is not entitled to pay for the period of absence (no work, no pay) but remains employed until a fair decision is taken. LRA referral periods are calendar days (Interpretation Act s.4); internal steps in this flow use working days.

Who is the employer. For placed workers earning above the BCEA earnings threshold (R269 600.90 a year from 1 May 2026), or placed for 3 months or less, or performing a genuine temporary service, the temporary employment service (TES) is the employer (s.198(2)) and runs the incapacity process; the client reports the concern. For workers below the threshold placed for more than 3 months, the client is deemed the employer (s.198A(3)(b); Assign Services v NUMSA, CC 2018) and must run the incapacity process itself; do not “request removal” as a substitute for that process. Public-service employers follow their bargaining council resolutions and the PILIR framework for ill health (verify).

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Employee Relations Officer (ERO, the case owner; in smaller organisations the HR manager); Line Manager (LM); HR Manager (HR); Occupational Health Practitioner (OHP, employer-appointed); Employee Assistance Programme provider (EAP); Employee Health and Wellness Representative (EHW, appointed under RRR Regs reg 3); COIDA Administrator (CA); Coach or Mediator (MED); Chairperson (CHR, independent of the matter); Appeal Chairperson (APC); Legal Adviser (LA); Payroll (PAY); Benefits Administrator (BEN, for group risk and retirement fund claims); Senior Sign-off (SSO, e.g. HR Director or COO; the Board chair where an executive is concerned); Board, Remuneration or Social and Ethics Committee (BOARD). The employee (EMP) and their representative (REP: a fellow employee or trade union representative, item 21(3)); together, “the employee party”. External: the employee’s treating medical practitioner (MP); family member or attorney acting for an incarcerated employee (FAM); Department of Correctional Services (DCS); trade union (TU); Compensation Fund (CF); retirement fund or insurer (FUND); CCMA or bargaining council (CCMA/BC).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be in place before the first case, because whether a performance standard was known and reasonably achievable (item 20(1)(b)(i), (iii)), whether the inherent requirements of a job were defined, and whether the employer had the means to accommodate, are all fixed by what existed before the problem arose.

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed by an employee yet, but the performance-awareness test in item 20(1)(b)(i) is decided here: an employee who was never given the standard is hard to dismiss for missing it.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: An employer with no benefits map may dismiss an employee who would otherwise have qualified for disability income, converting a manageable case into a claim for the lost benefit and an unfairness finding. Map benefits before the first case.

stages.title: Phase 1 — Identification, intake and classification
intro: Day 0 is the day any manager first sees a sustained problem: a performance shortfall, a pattern of absence or reduced capacity, news of an arrest, or a breakdown in working relationships. Phase 1 answers three questions by working day 5 (BP): is this incapacity or something else; if incapacity, which type; and does any special status change the process. It makes no finding.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Engage honestly in the first conversation; tell the employer if something is affecting their work if they want it taken into account; follow the sick-leave notification and certificate rules. An employee need not disclose a diagnosis at this stage, but should be told that the employer can only take into account what it knows.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: LM → ERO. ERO → LA (special status; can’t-or-won’t doubt). ERO → CA (work-related). ERO → EAP (with consent). ERO → TU. ERO → TES (only where the TES is the employer; see 1.6).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Two first-conversation errors recur: a manager who asks for a diagnosis or speculates about mental health (a POPIA and discrimination risk), and a manager who calls a performance or health problem “misconduct” in an email, which later makes the incapacity route look like a pretext.

stages.group: Phase 2 — Investigation and support, by type
stages.title: Track 2A — Poor work performance (after probation)
intro: Phase 2 is where most incapacity cases are won or lost. Each track gathers the facts its test needs and gives the support the Code expects, and each ends with a review that either closes the case, continues support, or passes the case to Phase 3. Only one track normally runs at a time; where a second cause emerges (a performance problem turns out to be medical), switch tracks in writing and tell the employee why.

The employer must show that the employee failed to meet a performance standard, that the employee knew or could reasonably be expected to know the standard, was given a fair opportunity to meet it, and that the standard was reasonably achievable (item 20(1)). Before dismissing, the employer must have given appropriate evaluation, instruction, training, guidance or counselling, and a reasonable period for improvement (item 19(1)).

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Attend meetings; engage with the PIP; use the support offered; say early if the support is not working or if a health or personal issue is affecting performance.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A PIP issued as a formality after the decision has in substance been made is easily exposed at arbitration. So is a standard that no one else in the team meets.

stages.group: Phase 2 — Investigation and support, by type
stages.title: Track 2B — Ill health and injury (including dependency)
intro: Under the Code the employer should investigate the extent of the incapacity; decide whether it is temporary or permanent; where a temporary absence is likely to be unreasonably long, investigate all alternatives short of dismissal; in permanent cases, look for alternative employment or adapt the duties or work circumstances (item 21(1)–(2)); a failure to investigate alternatives will rarely be justified. The employee must be allowed to state a case and be assisted by a trade union representative or fellow employee (item 21(3)). Degree and cause matter (item 21(4)); work-related cases carry a more onerous duty (item 21(5)).

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Notify absence and provide certificates; stay in contact as agreed; consent to, or explain a refusal to consent to, reasonable medical enquiries; attend OHP appointments; follow treatment and rehabilitation plans; take part in consultations; tell the employer about benefit claims and changes in condition.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Dismissing after sick leave runs out, without medical information or a consultation, is the classic unfair ill-health dismissal. So is relying on an OHP report the employee never saw or could not answer.

stages.group: Phase 2 — Investigation and support, by type
stages.title: Track 2C — Incarceration
intro: Imprisonment is a form of incapacity that may be temporary or permanent; the employer should assess its extent and investigate all alternatives short of dismissal (item 21(6)). The employer’s interest is the operational effect of the absence, not the guilt of the employee. The criminal matter is relevant only if the underlying conduct is itself workplace misconduct, or a conviction removes an inherent requirement of the job.

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Let the employer know of the detention as soon as possible, directly or through someone else; nominate a contact person; give realistic information about duration; respond to letters and make representations; tell the employer promptly on release.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Two errors decide most incarceration cases against employers: dismissing for “desertion” when the employer knew where the employee was, and deciding without asking the employee (through any available channel) for representations.

stages.group: Phase 2 — Investigation and support, by type
stages.title: Track 2D — Incompatibility
intro: Incompatibility, shown by an inability to work in harmony with the employer’s business culture or with fellow employees, can be a form of incapacity that justifies dismissal (item 21(7)). The Code gives no procedure, so this track follows the case law: the incompatibility must be real and attributable to the employee, the employee must be told specifically what is wrong and what is required, and must be given a fair opportunity to remedy it before dismissal is considered (CL: Erasmus v BB Bread, IC 1987; Wright v St Mary’s Hospital, IC 1992; Jabari v Telkom, LC 2006; Zeda Car Leasing t/a Avis Fleet v Van Dyk [2020] ZALAC 4; the IC and LC authorities to be verified).

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Engage with counselling, mediation and coaching; honour the behavioural agreement; raise grievances through the grievance procedure rather than through conflict.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Incompatibility is the easiest ground to abuse and the hardest to prove. “Not a cultural fit” without specifics, or a process begun after the employee lodged a grievance or complaint, is a strong signal of an automatically unfair or pretextual dismissal.

steps.label: 2D.1
steps.title: Protected-reason screen
steps.action: Before anything else, check whether the “incompatibility” may reflect race, gender, language, religion, culture, disability, age, pregnancy, union activity, a grievance, a harassment complaint or a protected disclosure. If it may, LA review; the matter cannot proceed as incompatibility until that risk is excluded.

stages.group: Phase 3 — Alternatives short of dismissal and the decision to proceed
stages.title: Phase 3 — Alternatives short of dismissal and the decision to proceed
intro: All four tracks converge here. The Code provides that the employer should investigate all possible alternatives short of dismissal for ill health and incarceration (item 21(1), (6)) and look for alternative employment or adapted duties in permanent incapacity (item 21(2)); a failure to do so will rarely be justified. For poor performance, the employer must be able to show that dismissal was an appropriate response (item 20(1)(b)(iv)). Phase 3 records that search and ends with a signed decision.

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Consider alternatives in good faith; make proposals; answer offers within the time given. An employee who unreasonably refuses a suitable alternative weakens a later unfairness claim.

stages.title: Phase 4 — The incapacity enquiry
intro: The enquiry is a structured opportunity for the employee to state a case before any dismissal decision (items 19(2), 21(3)). It is not a trial of fault: the questions are whether the incapacity exists, its extent and likely duration, whether the employer has done what is reasonable, and whether any alternative remains. It is run less adversarially than a disciplinary enquiry, but with the same attention to notice, disclosure, representation and reasons. The notice rule in the Misconduct flow is adopted: at least 48 hours and two full working days, with longer for complex matters (BP 5 working days).

steps.title: Rights to refer
steps.action: Dismissal for incapacity: refer an unfair dismissal dispute to the CCMA or a council with jurisdiction within 30 days of the date of dismissal or, if later, of the date on which the employer made a final decision to dismiss or to uphold the dismissal on appeal (s.191(1)(b)(i)); conciliation, then arbitration. All dismissal disputes, including automatically unfair ones (disability or another prohibited ground), must be referred within the same 30 days; after conciliation they go to the Labour Court (s.191(5)(b)(i)). Unilateral demotion or other action short of dismissal: unfair labour practice within 90 days (s.191(1)(b)(ii)). Unfair discrimination short of dismissal: within 6 months of the act or omission (EEA s.10(2)); if unresolved, to the Labour Court, or to CCMA arbitration where the employee earns below the BCEA earnings threshold or the parties consent (EEA s.10(6)). Late referral needs condonation.

intro: Every concern feeds one intake. Phase 1 decides whether the matter is incapacity at all and, if so, which of the four types; each type then runs its own Phase 2 track. referenceTables.section: §15 Corrections to existing GBS materials and drafting issues
rows: Refers to “the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal (Schedule 8)” and to “Schedule 8 — Code of Good Practice: Dismissal”
Schedule 8 was repealed on 4 September 2025. Cite the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294), items 14 to 21.
“Enhanced Code of Good Practice, 2025 — Updated incapacity and accommodation standards”

No instrument has that name. Replace with the 2025 Code, and add the EEA Code of Good Practice on the Employment of Persons with Disabilities (GN 1085, GG 39383, 9 November 2015) and the COIDA RRR Regs, 2026.
Incapacity defined as inability “through no fault of their own”

The phrase fits poor performance and ill health but not incarceration (which may follow the employee’s own conduct) or incompatibility. Define incapacity as an inability or unsuitability to meet the requirements of the job that does not arise from a culpable breach of a workplace rule.
Poor performance steps omit achievability and the warning

Add that the standard must be reasonably achievable (item 20(1)(b)(iii)); that the reasons for underperformance must be investigated (a health cause moves the case to ill health); that the PIP must warn that dismissal may follow, subject to the item 20(2) exception for managers and senior professionals.
Probation: “the standard of proof for poor performance is less onerous”

Item 18(2) refers to reasons that may be less compelling, not a lower standard of proof. Add item 17 (reasonable guidance), item 18(1) (representations before dismissal or extension) and item 15(2) (probation not to be used to avoid permanent status).
“Dismiss only where incapacity is permanent or of indefinite duration”; “temporary incapacity alone is insufficient basis for dismissal”

Too narrow. Item 21(1) contemplates dismissal where a temporary absence is likely to be unreasonably long and no alternative exists. Reword: dismissal may be considered where the incapacity is permanent, or temporary but likely to last an unreasonably long time, and alternatives are exhausted.
Work-related ill health: “presumption in favour of accommodation”; “preference for re-employment even if full restoration impossible”

No statutory presumption exists. State the item 21(5) rule (a more onerous duty to accommodate) and the RRR Regs duties, including notice to the Fund or Licensee before dismissal or a pay reduction (reg 10(1)(n)), the written dismissal report to the Chief Inspector and the Fund (reg 10(1)(m)), the resumption or inability-to-retain notice (reg 10(1)(o)) and 30-year retention of RRR reports (reg 10(1)(d)).
The EEA disability framework uses “unjustifiable hardship” (verify). Use that term and say what is weighed: cost, size and resources, effect on operations and others, safety.
No reference to benefits before dismissal
Add a mandatory benefits check (disability, income continuation, ill-health retirement) before any termination, so the employee is not dismissed out of cover.
Add item 21(4): counselling and rehabilitation may be appropriate for alcohol or drug dependency; relapse is assessed against the rehabilitation plan.
Incompatibility indicators include “refusal to adopt … ethical standards”, “disrespect”, “active obstruction of team efforts”

Refusal to follow rules, disrespect and obstruction are usually misconduct and should be charged as such. Incompatibility is an inability to work in harmony that is not a rule-breach. Add a protected-reason screen and an attribution test (is it the employee, or others?).
Incarceration: “Employers … may not treat the situation as desertion”

Correct in substance; add the source (item 21(6)), the no-work-no-pay position, leave options, contact through family or attorney, review at court dates, and the distinct case where a conviction removes an inherent requirement.
Consolidated checklist: “misconduct process considered separately” only for incarceration
Applies to all four types (the Redrafted policy already corrects this).
Records kept “for a minimum of three years”

Keep at least until referral, review and appeal periods and any litigation have ended, and in line with a retention schedule; health records from occupational exposure may need far longer retention under OHS regulations (verify). Store medical information separately (POPIA s.26).
Right to refer: CCMA or council “within 30 days of the date of dismissal”

Add: all dismissal disputes, including automatically unfair dismissals (disability, pregnancy), are referred within 30 days and go to the Labour Court after conciliation; the 30 days run from the date of dismissal or, if later, the employer’s final decision to dismiss or uphold the dismissal on appeal (s.191(1)(b)(i)); unfair labour practices (e.g. unilateral demotion) within 90 days; EEA unfair discrimination claims short of dismissal within 6 months (EEA s.10(2)), with CCMA arbitration available below the BCEA threshold or by consent (s.10(6)); condonation.
Ill-health step 2: “Request a comprehensive medical report: diagnosis …”

Ask for functional information, not a diagnosis, unless the diagnosis is necessary; obtain written consent; limit access (POPIA ss.26–27, 32(1)(f), 32(2); Health Information Regulations, 2026); consider the employee’s own doctor and an OHP (CL: Solomons, verify).
intro: Comparing the GBS Incapacity Management Policy, the Baseline and Redrafted incapacity policies and the Holistic Incapacity Policy presentation against the LRA, the 2025 Code, the EEA, the RRR Regs and case law turned up points that should be fixed before client use. This flow already reflects them. The Redrafted policy fixes several points in the original and should be the base for the update.

Managers should record effects on work, not speculate about health from appearance. Replace with work-related indicators.
“End-of-probation dismissals must be justified, preferably by documented job-related incapacity”
Item 18(2) and 15(1) allow decisions on performance and suitability; the point is that reasons must relate to the purpose of probation and the employee must be heard (item 18(1)).

Genuine illness-related absence belongs in the ill-health track (item 21), with medical input and the disability overlay; uncertified or false absence is misconduct. Managing sick leave as “poor performance” risks a disability-discrimination claim. Move these indicators to §3.

Add the RRR Regs reg 10(1) notices (10(1)(n) before dismissal or pay reduction; 10(1)(m) dismissal report and 10(1)(o) resumption notice after; 30-year retention under 10(1)(d)), and a cross-reference to the GBS COIDA flow.

referenceTables.title: Corrections to the Holistic Incapacity Policy presentation
referenceTables.section: §15 Corrections to existing GBS materials and drafting issues
rows: Incarceration case table: Khanye v Auditor General (2024) 5 BALR 530 (CCMA); “Eskom Ltd v CCMA & Njawuza (Labour Court JR2025/06, 2008)”; “[Unnamed case, Labour Court 2007]”

Verify every citation before use. A CCMA award is not binding precedent; the Eskom citation mixes a case number format with a 2008 date and describes the CCMA’s finding rather than the court’s; an unnamed case cannot be cited. Replace with verified Labour Court or Labour Appeal Court authority, or present the principles without citations.
SAMWU obo Solomons v City of Cape Town [2009] 18 SALGB … “The court held …”
The citation is to a bargaining council award, not a court. Describe it as an award and verify it.
Parexel International (Pty) Ltd v Chakane, Wilcocks v Khawula, Jansen, Mogomatsi

Parexel v Chakane ([2019] ZALAC 50), Jansen ([2020] ZALAC 37) and Mogomatsi (CA12/2022, LAC 2023) are verified. Present Jansen accurately: it does not require discipline to pause, and places the evidential burden on the employee to show that the illness negated capacity. Confirm the characterisation of Wilcocks (a dismissal following the employee’s acceptance of medical boarding) before relying on it as a general rule.
Re-employment preference for work-related incapacity is “a specific requirement”

The Code’s re-employment item is item 24(16), which deals with retrenchment. For work-related incapacity rely on item 21(5) and the RRR Regs; describe re-employment preference as best practice unless the RRR Regs require it (verify).
Cause of incapacity “may be unrelated to work (e.g. general illness, injury, imprisonment)”
Imprisonment is a separate form of incapacity under item 21(6), not a category of ill health.
Incompatibility scenarios: introverts vs extroverts; direct vs indirect communicators; high-context vs low-context communication

Differences in style are normal diversity and can be proxies for culture, language or ethnicity. They do not by themselves show an inability to work in harmony. Present them as causes of friction to be managed, and warn that relying on them for dismissal risks unfair discrimination.
Dictionary definition including legal incompatibility of laws
Not relevant to item 21(7); replace with the Code’s wording and the case-law requirements (attribution, specific notice, opportunity to remedy).
Incarceration: consider whether the relationship has become “intolerable”
Intolerability is the Code’s misconduct test (items 7, 9). For incarceration the question is whether the absence is unreasonably long and alternatives are exhausted (item 21(6)).

Item 21(7) recognises incompatibility but gives no procedure, leaving the requirements (specific notice, attribution, opportunity to remedy) to case law.

Item 21(4) uses “alcoholism or drug abuse”; modern practice speaks of substance use disorders or dependency, and the Code is silent on other dependencies.
